courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Resolve a relative path
questions.prompt: Your working directory is `/home/lee/project`. Where does `../notes` point?
questions.explanation: .. selects the parent directory before notes is resolved.

questions.label: Quote a value with spaces
questions.prompt: A variable holds `my report.txt`. Which command removes exactly that one file?
questions.explanation: Double quotes expand the variable and keep the spaces inside one argument; unquoted splits it into two names, single quotes pass the literal text `$name`.

questions.label: Separate output from errors
questions.prompt: `find / -name core 2>/dev/null` does what to the messages about unreadable directories?

choices.text: Discards them while ordinary results still print
Discards every line including the results
Writes them to a file called 2

questions.explanation: 2> redirects the error stream only, leaving standard output untouched.

questions.label: Trace a pipeline's exit status
questions.prompt: In `grep pattern file | sort`, which command's exit status does the shell report by default?

choices.text: sort, the last command in the pipeline
The highest status of the two

questions.explanation: A pipeline's status is the status of its final command unless pipefail is set.

questions.label: Search file contents recursively
questions.prompt: Which command lists files under the current tree whose contents mention `timeout`?
questions.explanation: grep -r reads file contents; find -name and ls match file names only.

questions.label: Read a permission string
questions.prompt: A file shows `-rw-r--r--` and belongs to another user. You are not root. What can you do?
questions.explanation: The last triplet applies to others: read, no write, no execute.

questions.label: Stop a process without losing its work
questions.prompt: A long job ignores Ctrl-C. Which signal asks it to shut down cleanly before you resort to force?
questions.explanation: SIGTERM can be handled, so a process can flush and exit; SIGKILL cannot be caught and loses in-flight work.

questions.label: Make a variable visible to a child
questions.prompt: Why does a script fail to see `API_URL` that you set with `API_URL=http://x` in your shell?

choices.text: It was never exported, so children do not inherit it

questions.explanation: Only exported variables enter a child process's environment.

questions.label: Follow a log for a pattern
questions.prompt: Which command prints new matching lines as a log grows?
questions.explanation: tail -f streams appended lines; grep needs line buffering to emit each match immediately.

questions.label: Diagnose a full disk that df disagrees about
questions.prompt: `df` reports a full disk but `du` on the mount finds far less. What is the usual cause?

choices.text: A deleted file still held open by a running process
A corrupt filesystem needing a rebuild

questions.explanation: Space is not released until the last descriptor closes, so the kernel still counts a deleted but open file.

questions.label: Choose a safe recovery order
questions.prompt: A service is down and the disk is full. Which step comes first?

choices.text: Free space from a known-safe location, then restart the service
Restart the service and watch whether it recovers

questions.explanation: Restarting into a full disk repeats the failure; recovering the resource first is what lets the restart hold.

questions.label: Make an investigation reproducible
questions.prompt: You fixed an incident with a chain of shell commands. What makes the work reusable rather than folklore?

choices.text: A recorded script with the checks and their expected output
Remembering the commands for next time

questions.explanation: A recorded script with its expected output can be rerun and reviewed; memory and screenshots cannot.

questions.label: Resolve a relative path
questions.prompt: From `/var/log/nginx`, which path does `../../tmp` reach?
questions.explanation: Two parent steps land on /var, and tmp is resolved from there.

questions.label: Quote a value with spaces
questions.prompt: What does `echo '$HOME'` print?
questions.explanation: Single quotes suppress expansion entirely.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Give a script a usable contract
questions.prompt: What does `set -euo pipefail` at the top of a script change?

choices.text: It stops on an error, an unset variable, or a failing pipeline stage
It enables verbose tracing of every command
It makes the script run as root

questions.explanation: Each flag turns a silent failure into a stop: -e on error, -u on unset variables, pipefail on a failing stage inside a pipeline.

questions.label: Handle arguments safely
questions.prompt: Inside a script, which form passes every argument through unchanged, including ones with spaces?
questions.explanation: Quoted "$@" expands to one word per argument; the others join or re-split them.

questions.label: Act on an exit status
questions.prompt: Which line runs `cleanup` only when `build` fails?
questions.explanation: || runs the right side when the left side exits non-zero.

questions.label: Return a value from a function
questions.prompt: How does a Bash function usefully hand a string back to its caller?

choices.text: It echoes the string and the caller captures it with $( )
It uses return with the string

questions.explanation: return carries only a small integer status; output capture is how a string travels.

questions.label: Clean up on any exit
questions.prompt: Which mechanism removes a temporary file whether the script succeeds, fails or is interrupted?
questions.explanation: An EXIT trap runs on normal and abnormal termination alike.

questions.label: Read a file line by line without mangling it
questions.prompt: Which loop preserves backslashes and leading spaces on each line?

choices.text: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file
for line in $(cat file); do ...; done
while read line; do ...; done < file

questions.explanation: IFS= keeps leading and trailing whitespace and -r stops backslash interpretation; word splitting breaks the for loop.

questions.label: Publish a file atomically
questions.prompt: A reader must never see a half-written config. Which approach guarantees that?

choices.text: Write to a temporary file on the same filesystem, then rename it over the target
Truncate the target and write into it
Write to the target and chmod it afterwards

questions.explanation: rename is atomic within a filesystem, so a reader sees either the old file or the new one.

questions.label: Make a script safe to rerun
questions.prompt: What makes a provisioning script idempotent?

choices.text: Running it twice leaves the same result as running it once
It refuses to run if it ran before

questions.explanation: Idempotence is about the end state, not about blocking or recording repeats.

questions.label: Find where a script went wrong
questions.prompt: Which change shows each command with its expanded arguments as it runs?
questions.explanation: -x traces execution; the others change failure behaviour.

questions.label: Run work in parallel and collect it
questions.prompt: You start three background jobs with &. What makes the script fail when any of them fails?

choices.text: wait on each process id and check each status
wait with no arguments and check $?
Nothing: background failures cannot be detected

questions.explanation: A bare wait returns the status of the last job only; waiting per process id surfaces each one.

questions.label: Keep a scheduled script from overlapping itself
questions.prompt: A cron script sometimes runs twice at once. Which fix prevents that?

choices.text: Take an exclusive lock, for example with flock, and exit when it is held

questions.explanation: A lock makes the constraint explicit; timing changes only make a collision less likely.

questions.label: Decide what a script should not do
questions.prompt: When does a shell script stop being the right tool?

choices.text: When it needs structured data, concurrency and real error types
When it grows past one hundred lines
When it calls more than three external commands

questions.explanation: Length and command count are not the limit; structured data, concurrency and error handling are where the shell's model runs out.

questions.label: Give a script a usable contract
questions.prompt: With `set -u`, what happens at `echo "$missing"` when `missing` was never set?

choices.text: The script exits with an error

questions.explanation: -u turns an unset variable into a failure rather than an empty expansion.

questions.label: Handle arguments safely
questions.prompt: A script is called with one argument `two words`. What does `echo $1` print compared with `echo "$1"`?

choices.text: Both print two words, but only the quoted form keeps it as one argument
Only the unquoted form prints anything

questions.explanation: Unquoted expansion re-splits on whitespace, which matters the moment the value is passed on.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Order synchronous, microtask and timer work
questions.prompt: A script logs A, schedules a promise callback logging B, and a zero-delay timer logging C. What order prints?
questions.explanation: Microtasks drain completely after the synchronous run and before the next timer task.

questions.label: Capture a loop variable
questions.prompt: A for loop with var creates three callbacks reading the counter. What do they log after the loop?
questions.explanation: var has function scope, so every callback closes over the same binding; let would create one per iteration.

questions.label: Explain property lookup
questions.prompt: An object has no own `toString`, yet calling it works. Why?

choices.text: Lookup walks the prototype chain until it finds the property

questions.explanation: Property access follows the prototype chain, which is how inherited methods resolve.

questions.label: Reason about await scheduling
questions.prompt: Where does the code after an `await` resume?

choices.text: In a microtask once the awaited value settles

questions.explanation: await suspends the function and schedules the continuation as a microtask.

questions.label: Run independent work concurrently
questions.prompt: Two independent fetches are awaited on consecutive lines. What changes with Promise.all?

choices.text: They run concurrently instead of one after the other

questions.explanation: Sequential awaits start the second request only after the first settles; Promise.all starts both and waits for the pair.

questions.label: Keep an error's origin
questions.prompt: You catch an error and rethrow `new Error('failed')`. What is lost?

choices.text: The original stack and message, unless you pass it as the cause

questions.explanation: A fresh Error starts a new stack; the cause option keeps the original attached.

questions.label: Move work off the main thread
questions.prompt: A one-second computation freezes the interface. What does a worker change?

choices.text: It runs on another thread, so rendering and input keep going
It defers the computation to idle time

questions.explanation: A worker removes the work from the thread that renders and handles input; the work itself takes the same time.

questions.label: Explain a growing heap
questions.prompt: A page holds a listener on a removed element and memory climbs. Why is the element not collected?

choices.text: The listener keeps a reference reachable, so it cannot be collected

questions.explanation: Reachability decides collection, and a live listener keeps a path to the element.

questions.label: Explain why a hot function slows down
questions.prompt: A hot function is called with objects of differing shapes and gets slower. What happened?

choices.text: Its inline caches went polymorphic, so the fast path was lost
The engine stopped optimising all code

questions.explanation: Consistent object shapes let a call site stay monomorphic; varied shapes force a slower lookup.

questions.label: Share memory between threads safely
questions.prompt: Two workers update the same SharedArrayBuffer slot. What makes the update correct?

choices.text: A plain assignment, since writes are ordered
Copying the buffer for each worker

questions.explanation: Plain reads and writes on shared memory race; atomics provide indivisible updates.

questions.label: Keep animation smooth under load
questions.prompt: Rendering on the main thread stutters during data processing. Which change keeps frames steady?

choices.text: Render from a worker with an OffscreenCanvas
Batch all drawing into one long task

questions.explanation: Moving rendering off the contended thread is what protects the frame budget.

questions.label: Handle a real scheduling bug
questions.prompt: A daily reminder fires an hour late twice a year. What is the underlying mistake?

choices.text: Storing a wall-clock time and treating it as a fixed offset across daylight saving
A clock drift on the server

questions.explanation: A wall-clock time needs its zone re-resolved per day; a fixed offset breaks at a transition.

questions.label: Order synchronous, microtask and timer work
questions.prompt: A promise callback schedules another promise callback. When does a pending zero-delay timer run?

choices.text: After the microtask queue is empty

questions.explanation: The loop drains microtasks fully, including ones queued by other microtasks, before the next task.

questions.label: Capture a loop variable
questions.prompt: Replacing var with let in that loop changes the logs to what?
questions.explanation: let creates a fresh binding per iteration, which each callback captures.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Explain why a value is assignable
questions.prompt: A function takes `{ name: string }`. You pass an object with `name` and `age`. What happens?

choices.text: It is accepted, because the type only requires name
It is rejected for the extra property
It is accepted only with a cast

questions.explanation: TypeScript is structural: a value with at least the required members fits. Excess property checks apply to fresh object literals only.

questions.label: Choose between unknown and any
questions.prompt: Why prefer `unknown` over `any` for a value parsed from JSON?

choices.text: unknown forces a check before use, any disables checking
They are identical to the compiler

questions.explanation: unknown keeps the value opaque until you narrow it; any removes checking entirely.

questions.label: Read a function contract
questions.prompt: What does `(items: readonly string[]) => void` promise the caller?

choices.text: The function will not modify the array it receives
The array contents are frozen at runtime
The caller must pass a literal array

questions.explanation: readonly is a compile-time contract about this reference; it does not freeze the object at runtime.

questions.label: Narrow a union
questions.prompt: After `if (typeof value === 'string')`, what is the type in the else branch of `string | number`?
questions.explanation: A successful narrowing removes the matched member from the remaining branch.

questions.label: Reason about generic assignability
questions.prompt: Why is `Array<Dog>` not safely assignable to `Array<Animal>` in a mutable position?

choices.text: Because you could then push a Cat into an array of Dogs
Because generics are invariant by syntax
Because Dog does not extend Animal structurally

questions.explanation: Mutability is what breaks covariance: a writable wider array would accept the wrong element.

questions.label: Predict an inferred type
questions.prompt: `const x = [1, 2, 3]` infers what, and why does `as const` change it?

choices.text: number[]; as const infers a readonly tuple of literals

questions.explanation: Inference widens literals in a mutable position; as const keeps the literal types and makes it readonly.

questions.label: Explain a declaration build failure
questions.prompt: A library builds fine but declaration emit fails on an exported function. What is the usual cause?

choices.text: Its inferred return type names a type that is not exported

questions.explanation: A public signature must be nameable in the emitted declarations, so the referenced type has to be exported too.

questions.label: Speed up a monorepo build
questions.prompt: What do project references give a large repository?

choices.text: Incremental builds where only changed projects rebuild

questions.explanation: References make the dependency graph explicit so tsc can rebuild only what changed.

questions.label: Explain a lost narrowing
questions.prompt: A property is narrowed, then used inside a callback, and the narrowing is gone. Why?

choices.text: The compiler cannot prove the property did not change before the callback ran

questions.explanation: Mutable properties lose narrowing across a function boundary; a local const captures it.

questions.label: Diagnose a slow type-check
questions.prompt: Type-checking a large project takes minutes. Which change usually helps most?

choices.text: Replacing deep conditional and mapped type chains on hot paths with explicit types

questions.explanation: Type-level computation dominates check time in large projects; strictness and target do not.

questions.label: Keep inference useful at scale
questions.prompt: Why annotate the return type of a widely used exported function?

choices.text: It stops a change from silently rippling through every caller's inferred types

questions.explanation: An explicit signature pins the contract, so a change becomes an error at the source rather than a surprise downstream.

questions.label: Choose the right level of type safety
questions.prompt: Where is a runtime check still required despite full type coverage?

choices.text: At every boundary where external data enters the program
Nowhere, types are checked at runtime

questions.explanation: Types describe the program's interior; data crossing a boundary has to be validated at runtime.

questions.label: Explain why a value is assignable
questions.prompt: Passing the object literal `{ name: 'a', age: 2 }` directly to that parameter does what?

choices.text: It is rejected by the excess property check on fresh literals
It is accepted like a variable would be

questions.explanation: Fresh object literals get an extra check that a named variable does not.

questions.label: Choose between unknown and any
questions.prompt: What does a variable of type `never` mean at a point in the code?
questions.explanation: never is the empty type, so reaching it is a contradiction the compiler can use for exhaustiveness.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Place state correctly
questions.prompt: Two sibling components need the same value. Where should it live?

choices.text: In their nearest common ancestor, or a store both read
In module scope as a mutable variable

questions.explanation: A single owner above both keeps them consistent; duplicates drift and module globals leak across trees.

questions.label: Design a component boundary
questions.prompt: A component takes fifteen boolean props. What does that usually signal?

choices.text: Several components are hiding inside one
A need for better prop documentation
That the component should be memoised

questions.explanation: A wide boolean surface is variation that wants separate components or composition.

questions.label: Decide what crosses the boundary
questions.prompt: Why not pass a database row straight to a client component?

choices.text: It ships fields the client must not see and couples the interface to the schema

questions.explanation: The boundary is where you choose a shape: exposure and coupling are the costs, not speed.

questions.label: Choose a rendering strategy
questions.prompt: Content is identical for every visitor and changes hourly. Which strategy fits?
questions.explanation: Shared, slowly changing content is cacheable; per-request rendering pays for nothing.

questions.label: Reason about a cache key
questions.prompt: A list and its detail view disagree after an edit. What is the usual cause?

choices.text: The mutation invalidated one cache key and not the other

questions.explanation: Two views are two entries; correctness depends on invalidating every key the write affects.

questions.label: Model an async interaction
questions.prompt: Why model a form as a state machine rather than several booleans?

choices.text: Impossible combinations such as loading and error together stop existing
It removes the need for validation

questions.explanation: A machine encodes which states exist and which transitions are legal; independent booleans allow contradictions.

questions.label: Handle an optimistic update
questions.prompt: An optimistic update succeeds locally but the request fails. What must the code do?

choices.text: Roll back to the previous value and surface the failure

questions.explanation: Optimism is a loan against the server; a failure has to return the interface to a truthful state.

questions.label: Ship a risky change safely
questions.prompt: Which technique limits the blast radius of a risky frontend change?

choices.text: Releasing behind a flag to a small share of traffic first

questions.explanation: Progressive exposure bounds who is affected and lets you stop; timing and testing do not bound it.

questions.label: Judge a microfrontend split
questions.prompt: When does splitting an application across teams pay for itself?

choices.text: When independent deployment is worth the runtime and duplication costs
Whenever the codebase passes a size threshold
When each page has its own route

questions.explanation: The split buys deployment independence and charges runtime complexity; size alone is not the trade.

questions.label: Decide what belongs at the edge
questions.prompt: Which work belongs in edge middleware rather than the origin?

choices.text: Cheap request-shaping such as redirects, locale and auth checks

questions.explanation: Edge code runs before the origin with tight limits; it shapes requests rather than doing heavy work.

questions.label: Keep a mutation honest
questions.prompt: After a server mutation, what keeps the client view correct?

choices.text: Revalidating the data the mutation affected

questions.explanation: The mutation has to name what it invalidated; a full reload is a blunt version of the same idea.

questions.label: Defend an architecture decision
questions.prompt: What makes an architecture decision record useful a year later?

choices.text: The constraints and rejected alternatives, not just the choice
A diagram of the final system

questions.explanation: The reasoning is what lets a later reader tell whether the constraints still hold.

questions.label: Place state correctly
questions.prompt: That shared value is only used by one sibling after a refactor. What should happen?

choices.text: Move it back down into the component that uses it
Promote it to a global store

questions.explanation: State belongs as low as it can sit; leaving it high keeps unrelated renders coupled.

questions.label: Design a component boundary
questions.prompt: Which prop signature better expresses three mutually exclusive appearances?
questions.explanation: A union makes the exclusivity impossible to violate; three booleans allow contradictions.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Design a command line contract
questions.prompt: What should a tool print to standard output when its result is meant to be piped?

choices.text: Only the machine-readable result, with progress on standard error

questions.explanation: Separating streams is what lets a tool be composed; progress on stdout corrupts the pipe.

questions.label: Choose between a regex and a parser
questions.prompt: Why rename a symbol with an abstract syntax tree rather than a regular expression?

choices.text: Only the tree distinguishes the symbol from a string or comment that looks like it

questions.explanation: A parser knows what each token means; a pattern matches text wherever it appears.

questions.label: Pick a build target
questions.prompt: What does setting a lower build target change?

choices.text: More syntax is transpiled and polyfilled, so bundles grow

questions.explanation: The target decides how much the compiler rewrites, which shows up as output size and speed.

questions.label: Explain a bundle that is too large
questions.prompt: Tree shaking leaves an unused module in the bundle. What usually prevents its removal?

choices.text: A side effect the bundler cannot prove is unused

questions.explanation: Elimination needs proof of purity; an unmarked side effect forces the bundler to keep the module.

questions.label: Make a watch loop fast
questions.prompt: What makes an incremental rebuild fast after one file changes?

choices.text: Reusing cached results for everything the change cannot affect

questions.explanation: The dependency graph bounds the work; parallelism only speeds up work you still do.

questions.label: Debug a minified stack
questions.prompt: A production stack trace points at column 4,000 of one line. What restores the original location?

choices.text: A source map published alongside the bundle

questions.explanation: A source map is the mapping back to the authored file, line and column.

questions.label: Explain a test that only fails in a suite
questions.prompt: A test passes alone and fails in the suite. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: Shared state left behind by another test

questions.explanation: Order dependence comes from state that outlives a test; isolation or explicit cleanup fixes it.

questions.label: Cache a task correctly
questions.prompt: What must a task cache key include to be safe?

choices.text: Every input that changes the output, including configuration and tool version
The task name and the date

questions.explanation: A cache is only correct when its key covers all inputs; missing one returns stale output.

questions.label: Judge a lint rule
questions.prompt: When is a lint rule worth its noise?

choices.text: When it catches a real defect class and has few false positives
When it enforces a team's formatting taste

questions.explanation: Value is the defect class it prevents against the cost of its false positives.

questions.label: Expose a tool to an agent safely
questions.prompt: What matters most when exposing a build tool to an automated agent?

choices.text: A narrow, declared surface with explicit permissions
Returning as much context as possible

questions.explanation: A tool the agent can misuse is a liability; a narrow declared surface bounds what can happen.

questions.label: Make a performance budget stick
questions.prompt: Which budget actually prevents regressions?

choices.text: One enforced in continuous integration that fails the build

questions.explanation: An unenforced budget is a wish; the failing build is what stops the regression landing.

questions.label: Sequence a toolchain migration
questions.prompt: How do you migrate a large build to a new bundler with least risk?

choices.text: Run both and compare output and timings until the new one matches
Switch entirely on a quiet day
Rewrite the configuration from scratch first

questions.explanation: Running in parallel gives evidence of equivalence before you depend on it.

questions.label: Design a command line contract
questions.prompt: What should a tool's exit status be when it finds problems it was asked to report?

choices.text: Non-zero, so a script can act on it
Always zero, since it ran successfully
Zero unless the tool itself crashed

questions.explanation: The status is the machine-readable verdict; scripts branch on it.

questions.label: Choose between a regex and a parser
questions.prompt: A codemod must keep comments and formatting. What does that require?

choices.text: A parser that records trivia and a printer that re-emits it

questions.explanation: Comments and whitespace survive only if the tool represents them and prints them back.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each stage of this course, so the check can place you at any stage rather than guessing past the ones it never sampled.

questions.label: Estimate a workload
questions.prompt: A service handles 8,600,000 requests a day, roughly evenly spread. What is the average rate?
questions.explanation: A day is about 86,400 seconds, so 8.6 million requests average roughly 100 per second.

questions.label: Tell two consistency models apart
questions.prompt: A read immediately after a successful write returns the old value. Which model permits this?
questions.explanation: Only eventual consistency allows a read to trail a completed write; the others forbid it.

questions.label: Recognise what blocks horizontal scaling
questions.prompt: A web tier keeps session data in process memory. What breaks when you add a second instance?

choices.text: Requests routed to the other instance lose the session

questions.explanation: State held in one process is invisible to the others, so scaling out needs the state moved to a shared store or the routing pinned.

questions.label: Check quorum overlap
questions.prompt: With five replicas, a write quorum of three and a read quorum of two, can a read miss the newest committed write?

choices.text: Yes, because three plus two does not exceed five

questions.explanation: Overlap needs W + R greater than N; three plus two equals five, so a read set can avoid every writer.

questions.label: Recognise skew
questions.prompt: Sharding by customer identifier leaves one shard at 80% CPU and the others idle. What is happening?

choices.text: A few very large customers concentrate load on one shard
The shard count is too high

questions.explanation: Partitioning by an entity with a skewed size distribution concentrates load regardless of hashing quality.

questions.label: Reason about replication lag
questions.prompt: Reads are served from an asynchronous replica. A user updates a profile and immediately reloads. What can they see?

choices.text: Their old profile, until the replica catches up

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication acknowledges the write before the replica applies it, so a following read can trail.

questions.label: Coordinate state with event publication
questions.prompt: A service commits a row and then publishes an event. The process dies in between. What does the outbox pattern change?

choices.text: The event is written in the same transaction and published later by a reader
The publish happens before the commit
Events are dropped when the process dies

questions.explanation: Writing the event with the data makes the pair atomic; a separate reader then publishes, so a crash cannot lose one half.

questions.label: Protect a dependency under failure
questions.prompt: A downstream service starts timing out and your latency climbs. What does a circuit breaker do?

choices.text: Stops calling it for a period so callers fail fast and the dependency can recover
Queues requests until the dependency returns

questions.explanation: Failing fast sheds load from a struggling dependency; retries and unbounded queues add to it.

questions.label: Choose a limiter for bursty traffic
questions.prompt: Clients send short bursts within a fair long-run rate. Which limiter admits the burst without raising the average?

choices.text: A token bucket with a burst size

questions.explanation: A token bucket accumulates allowance up to the burst size while bounding the sustained rate.

questions.label: Choose a fan-out strategy
questions.prompt: A social feed has a few accounts with millions of followers. Which approach handles them?

choices.text: Fan out on write for ordinary accounts and read-time merge for the huge ones
Fan out on write for everyone

questions.explanation: Writing millions of copies per post is the cost that forces a hybrid; ordinary accounts stay cheap on write.

questions.label: Guarantee ordering a user can see
questions.prompt: Two messages sent by one user must never appear out of order. What gives that cheaply?

choices.text: A per-conversation sequence assigned by the server
A global total order across all conversations

questions.explanation: Ordering is only observable within a conversation, so a per-conversation sequence is enough and a global order is far more costly.

questions.label: Defend a design under load
questions.prompt: You claim a design survives a tenfold traffic increase. What evidence makes that credible?

choices.text: Named bottleneck, its measured limit, and what changes when it is reached
A statement that the services scale horizontally

questions.explanation: A defensible claim names the limiting resource with a number and the response when it binds.

questions.label: Estimate a workload
questions.prompt: Peak traffic is five times the average of 100 requests per second, and each request takes 20 ms. Roughly how many concurrent requests are in flight at peak?
questions.explanation: Little's law: 500 per second times 0.02 seconds is about 10 in flight.

questions.label: Tell two consistency models apart
questions.prompt: Which guarantee does read-your-writes add over plain eventual consistency?

choices.text: A client always sees its own completed writes
Every client sees the same order of writes

questions.explanation: Read-your-writes is a session guarantee about the writer's own reads, not a global ordering.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each level from A1 to B2, so the check can place you at any level rather than stopping at the highest one it sampled. Reading and grammar only: speaking and listening are assessed inside lessons.

questions.label: A1: identify a meeting time
questions.prompt: Read: „Der Kurs beginnt am Montag um neun Uhr.“ Wann beginnt der Kurs?
questions.explanation: Montag is Monday and neun Uhr is nine o'clock.

questions.label: A1: match a verb to its subject
questions.prompt: Choose the form: „Ich ___ in Berlin.“
questions.explanation: First person singular takes the -e ending.

questions.label: A1: choose a polite opening
questions.prompt: You enter a shop in the morning. Which greeting fits?
questions.explanation: Gute Nacht is for leaving at night and Tschüss is a goodbye.

questions.label: A2: interpret a changed arrangement
questions.prompt: Read: „Der Termin am Dienstag fällt aus. Wir treffen uns stattdessen am Donnerstag.“ Was gilt?
questions.explanation: fällt aus cancels Tuesday and stattdessen introduces the replacement day.

questions.label: A2: place a past tense
questions.prompt: Complete: „Gestern ___ ich einen Film gesehen.“
questions.explanation: sehen forms the perfect with haben; bin is for verbs of motion and change of state.

questions.label: A2: ask for a change politely
questions.prompt: You must move an appointment. Which sentence asks politely?
questions.explanation: The subjunctive könnten makes it a request rather than an announcement.

questions.label: B1: follow an argument
questions.prompt: Read: „Das Angebot klingt gut, allerdings sind die Kosten zu hoch.“ Was meint der Autor?

choices.text: He likes it but rejects it on cost

questions.explanation: allerdings introduces the reservation that carries the writer's real position.

questions.label: B1: express a condition
questions.prompt: Complete: „Wenn ich mehr Zeit ___, würde ich Italienisch lernen.“
questions.explanation: The unreal condition needs the subjunctive hätte to match würde.

questions.label: B1: read register
questions.prompt: Which closing belongs in a formal email?
questions.explanation: The other two are informal sign-offs for people you know.

questions.label: B2: detect an implied stance
questions.prompt: Read: „Der Vorschlag ist zweifellos ambitioniert – ob er finanzierbar ist, steht auf einem anderen Blatt.“ Wie steht der Autor dazu?
questions.explanation: The idiom steht auf einem anderen Blatt sets the funding question aside as unresolved.

questions.label: B2: handle reported speech
questions.prompt: Report this: „Ich komme später.“ → Er sagte, ___.
questions.explanation: Reported speech in careful written German uses Konjunktiv I.

questions.label: B2: structure a written argument
questions.prompt: Which opening sets up an argued position?

choices.text: Im Folgenden möchte ich begründen, warum …

questions.explanation: It announces a claim and its justification rather than a topic or a list.

questions.label: A1: identify a meeting time
questions.prompt: Read: „Wir treffen uns um halb acht.“ Wie spät ist das?
questions.explanation: halb acht is half an hour before eight, not after.

questions.label: A1: match a verb to its subject
questions.prompt: Choose the form: „Du ___ sehr gut Deutsch.“
questions.explanation: Second person singular takes -st, with the stem vowel change.

courses.scope_note: Twelve short questions, three for each level from A1 to B2, so the check can place you at any level rather than stopping at the highest one it sampled. Reading and grammar only: speaking and listening are assessed inside lessons.

questions.label: A1: identify a meeting time
questions.prompt: Leggi: «Il corso inizia lunedì alle nove.» Quando inizia?
questions.explanation: lunedì is Monday and alle nove is at nine.

questions.label: A1: match a verb to its subject
questions.prompt: Scegli la forma: «Io ___ a Roma.»
questions.explanation: First person singular of -are verbs ends in -o.

questions.label: A1: choose a polite opening
questions.prompt: You enter a shop in the morning. Which greeting fits?
questions.explanation: Buonanotte is for leaving at night and the third is an informal goodbye.

questions.label: A2: interpret a changed arrangement
questions.prompt: Leggi: «L'incontro di martedì è annullato. Ci vediamo invece giovedì.» Qual è la situazione?
questions.explanation: annullato cancels Tuesday and invece introduces the replacement day.

questions.label: A2: place a past tense
questions.prompt: Completa: «Ieri ___ visto un film.»
questions.explanation: vedere forms the passato prossimo with avere.

questions.label: A2: ask for a change politely
questions.prompt: You must move an appointment. Which sentence asks politely?
questions.explanation: The conditional potremmo makes it a request rather than a decision already taken.

questions.label: B1: follow an argument
questions.prompt: Leggi: «La proposta è interessante, tuttavia i costi sono troppo alti.» Cosa pensa l'autore?

choices.text: He likes it but rejects it on cost

questions.explanation: tuttavia introduces the reservation that carries the writer's real position.

questions.label: B1: express a condition
questions.prompt: Completa: «Se ___ più tempo, studierei il tedesco.»
questions.explanation: The unreal condition takes the imperfect subjunctive with the conditional.

questions.label: B1: read register
questions.prompt: Which closing belongs in a formal email?
questions.explanation: The other two are warm closings for people you know.

questions.label: B2: detect an implied stance
questions.prompt: Leggi: «La proposta è senza dubbio ambiziosa; se sia sostenibile, è un altro discorso.» Qual è la posizione?
questions.explanation: è un altro discorso sets the feasibility question aside as unresolved.

questions.label: B2: handle reported speech
questions.prompt: Riporta: «Arrivo più tardi.» → Ha detto che ___.
questions.explanation: Reported speech after a past verb shifts a future intention to the past conditional.

questions.label: B2: structure a written argument
questions.prompt: Which opening sets up an argued position?
questions.explanation: It announces a claim and its justification rather than a topic or a list.

questions.label: A1: identify a meeting time
questions.prompt: Leggi: «Ci vediamo alle sette e mezza.» Che ora è?
questions.explanation: e mezza adds half an hour to the stated hour.

questions.label: A1: match a verb to its subject
questions.prompt: Scegli la forma: «Tu ___ molto bene l'italiano.»
questions.explanation: Second person singular of -are verbs ends in -i.
